newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Obstacles still delay oil-for-food plan, U.N. says.
newsitem.headline: Obstacles still delay oil-for-food plan, U.N. says.

text.p: Conditions are still not ripe to begin implementing an "oil-food-food" plan signed by Iraq and the United Nations in May, the U.N. official overseeing the operation said on Wednesday.

Speaking to reporters after briefing the Security Council in private, Under-Secretary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan said: "We are not looking for perfect conditions in which to operate. But we will insist on certain minimum conditions to be established on the ground before we can consider starting this whole process."
"We are not yet satisfied that we are there," he said.

He was referring to a deal under which Baghdad would be able to sell $2 billion of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help offset the effect on ordinary Iraqis of sanctions imposed after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Arrangements to launch the plan were close to completion when Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country at the end of August to back one side in an inter-Kurdish conflict.
Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali announced on Sept. 1 that security conditions prevented the deployment of U.N. staff to monitor the plan on the ground.

Gharekhan said the main remaining obstacles concerned the safety and freedom of movement of U.N. personnel and employees of non-governmental organisations in the north, and Iraq's wish for new local U.N. staff to be hired to replace those already working for the United Nations.
"The local staff in the north feel very insecure about their position," he said.
Diplomats said Iraq wanted 36 to 48 hours' notice before any foreign aid workers could move from one place to another.

"We have spoken to the government of Iraq about at least the perceived lack of security on the part of the local staff," Gharekhan said. "And we continue to have discussions ... on ways and means of reassuring the local staff."

He noted that under the May 20 agreement between Iraq and the United Nations freedom of movement was guaranteed for U.N. personnel. "There are some questions on this still to be resolved," Gharekhan said.
Confirming that Iraq also wanted some existing local U.N. employees fired and replaced, presumably by government-vetted staff, he said:

"One of Iraq's suggestions is that we should recruit new staff altogether. While this may have to be done, I do not know," Gharekhan added. But if it did become necessary, it would be another delaying factor, he said.

He gave no precise figures, saying only there were "a couple of hundred working with us ... but just for the north we will have to recruit several hundred more. So we are talking about fairly large numbers here."

Gharekhan said the secretary-general "who has very personally engaged himself in this question, would like to be in a position to submit his report (saying the plan could proceed) to the Security Council the soonest that he can."
A senior Security Council source said it appeared as if hardliners in Iraq who had opposed the initial oil-for-food plan were "making their weight felt."
Another envoy said he expected little movement on the plan until after the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election, suggesting Boutros-Ghali did not want the deal to become an issue in the campaign.
